speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity concerning the deplorable lack of low cost housing in Canada.
Whereas this government has failed to provide low cost housing, confirming that the lack of supply of decent, reasonably-priced shelter is not an accidental by-product of market forces but a deliberate policy; in view of the fact that house purchasing costs have risen over 14 per cent over last year across the country, for example in the district of Coquitlam a representative net profit was over $14,000 per lot; in view of the fact that the federal government is standing idly by while the government in British Columbia sells off at large profits housing estates built with federal funds intended for low-rental housing; and in view of the fact that experts now charge that the federal government is deliberately discouraging investment in low-cost housing in order to make capital available for extravagant, conspicuous projects like the Mackenzie Valley pipeline, which is ecologically and socially venal
May 26, 1976

and economically beneficial only to the large resources companies; I move, seconded by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn):
That this House condemn the government for its cruel policy of deliberately denying working Canadians the shelter to which their resourcefulness and productivity entitles them; and instruct this government to introduce legislation to correct this distortion immediately, and at the same time to plug loopholes in the National Housing Act, in order to guarantee that federal funds alloted to low-rental housing are used for the purpose intended.

With regard to the second point, the hon. gentleman used the phrase "the minister taped" a program. In fact, I did attend a press conference in the press lock-up yesterday afternoon prior to delivering the budget speech. At that time I answered questions from members of the press who subsequent to that, of course, remained in the lock-up until I rose to my feet to deliver the speech at eight o'clock. I am advised that for at least 20 years, if not longer, it has been the practice that members of the press gallery be admitted in advance for a briefing during the lock-up proceedings, and that it has also been the practice at eight o'clock for the press to be free to use the information then for the purpose of filing their reports whether it be through the written media or put out through the electronic media.
The hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby contacted me last Friday with a number of requests concerning the practice that had taken place for advance briefings in respect of selected members of the opposition, as opposed to the press, who would be present prior to delivery of the budget statement. The member pointed out, I think with some reason, that the press were at liberty to make public the briefing once the budget speech had commenced, but that
May 26, 1976

under the practice which had been operative for some time, members of the opposition were not permitted to comment on it until after the Minister of Finance had completed his speech.
The hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby made the point that surely it would be common sense and appropriate that members of parliament should be at liberty, as are members of the press, to comment from eight o'clock on upon what they had learned in the course of the budget briefing. I considered that over the weekend my staff advised the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby and, I am advised by the staff, also the Leader of the Opposition and other parties, that they would be free to do so. I am informed that, acting on this advice, the hon. member for York-Simcoe immediately after eight o'clock took advantage of it to put his own interpretation on the budget at 8.15.
The point is that if the hon. gentleman is to be entitled to make his comments, as I agree, immediately after eight o'clock, it seems to be equally clear that I should be entitled to have my comments put on the air. To do otherwise would be to have put the press in the position of being able to comment on the budget speech while it is being given, and to give the opposition the opportunity to comment on the budget speech while it is being given, but not to permit the deliverer of the speech to have his views expressed at the same time. So, Mr. Speaker, I conceded right away that this is a change in practice. It seems to me to have been a sensible change in practice. In the first place, it makes it possible for the opposition spokesmen to comment on the speech and for my views to be made known in that manner.
In connection with the distribution of the copies, I obviously did not have direct administrative control of the manner in which they would be distributed. However, I agree essentially that they should be delivered to members as soon as possible. I suggest that this procedure, based on a collection of precedents and conventions which have arisen around this, obviously is one area in which our whole budget procedure should be changed. It seems to me that by enabling statements to be made outside the House while the speech is going on, we are really debasing the procedure here in this chamber. There are several options in this regard. One is the notion that we should come back to the custom, which I understand from the hon. member for Mississauga was the case when his father occupied my present portfolio, of locking up the press until 9.15, 9.30 or until the minister had finished.
It seems to me that there would be no particular value in reverting to that practice. I suggest a change should take place in the procedures of the House so that we can have really a more current debate dealing with the budget speech when given. My present preference in respect of the budget statement would be to have all the proceedings of the House of Commons broadcast from the House through the media of television or radio broadcasting.
Since the budget statement is a lengthy and closely reasoned argument with regard to the state of the economy and what should take place, it seems to me that the budgetary statement should be made available in written form, in advance, and that we should then find procedures by which members would be able to debate orally on its contents under appropriate safeguards with regard to
Oral Questions
advance information. That is the background of the situation.
I come back again to the fact that I was yielding to an opposition request to improve procedures in dealing with the budget speech. I regret, in particular, that members on that side-and indeed I apologize to colleagues on my side-were not given copies of the budget statement or that they were not available to them as the statement was being given. The conclusion I draw from it is that this is one of the areas in which the ancient procedures which have gathered around this practice should be re-examined. We should see if we can find some twentieth century way of dealing with this matter.

Mr. Speaker, I have a few brief remarks. Unfortunately, last night's presentation of the budget address was hollow and unreal. First of all, I would like to say that I, personally, having participated in budget addresses for many years, have always felt that the Minister of Finance is addressing the House on these occasions. He is speaking to the House, not to the media or not to outside persons at all. This is merely another instance where I think well-meaning people actually downgrade and denigrate the status of this House.
It is not so many years ago that members of the opposition were allowed a period of prebriefing which the press has had for years. I recall that it is not so many years ago, either, that the press could release information only when the minister finished reading the budget address. If one went back to that practice, there would be none of this so called argy-bargy that is going on at present. If the press and the media have access to the air waves and to the television screens immediately after eight o'clock, then, naturally, there is pressure by members of the opposition who may have had an opportunity to see the budget to seek the same access.
Then the minister comes along and says that if the media have access and so has the opposition, why should he not have it. In other words, what tail wags the whole dog? I suggest to you, sir, that merely the fact the media have been allowed to comment on the budget immediately at eight o'clock has been at the root of this difficulty. In my view, the answer is not to put this on the television screen. It was tried at Queen's Park some three years ago. The provincial treasurer spoke at that time for the same length of time as did the minister last night, for 90 minutes or more, and the total audience was lost insofar as the budget was concerned. No minister can hold an audience for 90 minutes, particularly with the type of budget that is sometimes delivered.
It is my suggestion, as a means of improving the procedure, that if there is to be a lengthy budget statement, the minister, within the rules as they now stand, should indicate that he will make a short address, seek the leave of the House to table his budgetary statements, then merely give

the highlights and sit down. The document will have been in the hands of the opposition and the opposition spokesmen, instead of having to wait until ten o'clock to make their comments to the press-as was done last night- could wait, as I have done in the past, until the minister had finished his comments on the budget.
I suggest that if we are going to pay attention to the media, the national audience is lost if it has to watch the whole proceeding. This is my suggestion regarding how these proceedings could be shortened. The budgetary statement and the accompanying documents would be in the hands of hon. members, there could be a statement and questions, and then debate could start by ten o'clock. I offer that suggestion.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to raise a question of privilege resulting from the question I raised earlier. I have two short examples. One is a case which arose in 1936 in the British House of Commons. At that time Mr. Thomas, the colonial secretary, merely made a remark to a member of parliament of his own party, a Mr. Butt, that taxes may increase on tobacco and beer, following which he went into the House to read his speech. Later it was reported. In cabinet next morning he realized his indiscretion and resigned. It was laid down in Keith's book on constitutional law that there is a fundamental principle behind the doctrine of secrecy when a budget is drafted. The idea is not only to avoid evil, but to avoid the appearance of evil. The idea behind the whole thing is that a leak might permit someone to benefit from the information.
Then there is a second case, that of Sir Hugh Dalton in 1945. When he was walking into the chamber, he spoke to a Mr. Carvel, a newspaper reporter for the Star in England, and made some remark about taxes on sugar. After some

My dear Prime Minister,
In view of the incident which was raised today in the House I think it is my duty to offer you my resignation. If you accept it I shall continue, though now outside its ranks, to do my utmost to support the government-
In reply, the late Sir Winston Churchill wrote the following:
I realize that this indiscretion in itself did not result in any action detrimental to the state, but the principle of the inviolability of the budget is of the highest importance and the discretion of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, who necessarily receives many confidential communications, must be beyond question.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we must not consider this matter hastily and dismiss it. A special committee was set up at that time, and this is what they said:

speechtext:
1.	What is the maximum concentration of the radioactive gas radon which is presently considered by the Atomic Energy Control Board to be permissible without causing a public health hazard?
2.	Does the Atomic Energy Control Board have any plans or proposals for reducing, or otherwise altering, the current safety standard and, if so (a) what will become the maximum permissible safe level of radon concentration (b) on what date will the new standard be adopted (c) what is the purpose of and reasons for changing the existing standard?

speakeroldname: Mr. Maurice Foster (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: ATOMIC ENERGY CONTROL BOARD-CONCENTRATION OF RADIOACTIVE GAS RADON
speechtext:
The Atomic Energy Control Board reports as follows: 1. The maximum permissible concentration of radon in air, as of other radioactive isotopes, is derived from the maximum permissible doses of ionizing radiation specified in the Atomic Energy Control Regulations. In the case of radon almost all of the dose comes from the radioactive "daughter" products produced by the decay of radon. Depending on the rate of change of air in a particular room or space, the amount of dust, and other factors, the amount of these daughter products present may be equal to or considerably less than that which results from radioactive equilibrium. Assuming radioactive equilibrium, the worst case, the maximum permissible concentrations, for members of the general public, are: (a) 1 picocurie per litre (above natural background) for continuous occupancy (in a private dwelling); (b) 3 picocuries per litre (above natural background) for 40 hours per week occupancy (public buildings or business premises). The naturally occurring background in dwellings in the Port Hope region range from 0.5 to 3 picocuries per litre. Measurements made in buildings in Port Hope indicate that the daughter products are present only to 20 to 40 per cent of that which would result with radio-active equilibrium. The maximum permissible concentration for radon varies inversely with the per cent of equilibrium of the daughter products. If, for example, the daughter products are present to only 25 per cent of equilibrium the maximum permissible concentrations are (a) 4 picocuries per litre (continuous); (b) 12 picocuries per litre (40 hours per week occupancy).
2.	The Atomic Energy Control Board does not have any plans for reducing, or otherwise altering, the maximum permissible doses of ionizing radiation specified in the Atomic Energy Control Regulations.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE

speechtext: The House resumed, from Tuesday, May 25, consideration of the motion of Mr. Allmand that Bill C-84, to amend the Criminal Code in relation to the punishment for murder and certain other serious offences, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the conclusion of the business at six o'clock yesterday I had embarked upon a discussion about the causes of crime and also about the arguments those of us on the abolition side of this issue have made. The entire debate, in a sense, deflects the public mind away from dealing realistically with the subject of murder and with other crime.
With regard to the argument dealing with the causes of crime, the great tragedy in this country continues to be that we do not take a realistic view of how to reduce anti-social behaviour. By concentrating on whether we hang or do not hang, I do not think we make much of a contribution in either direction in terms of the reduction of the murder rate. If we go back to capital punishment, I have no doubt that there will be a public storm to remove hanging again because then the media will concentrate not on the victims of crime but on murderers. The media will give us three pages dealing with a murderer's last hours, what his last meal was, how the priest led him down to the scaffold and how the murderer's face went blue in the agony of the whole thing.
I believe the public mood will turn, and I have no illusions about the public mood. I am satisfied that a majority in this country favour the return of the death penalty, and that in my own constituency there is a majority which favours the death penalty. I must apologize to those constituents who disagree with the position I take, but I believe they understand that position. I believe they understood it in the last election in 1974 when I was re-elected. I made my position clear in 1972 and in 1974, and I am making it clear again today.
I do not expect a man who runs for parliament to change the views he holds at the time he runs depending on the winds which may be blowing back and forth across his riding. I have taken a very strong position in this House in terms of removal of abortion from the Criminal Code, but I would say that if a person running for parliament believed in the principle of the right to life on that issue and made his position clear in his riding, I, as his constituent, would not expect him to come to this place and change his vote on that fundamental matter of conscience. That is the principle we have to abide by, and that is the tradition of this place.
It is absolutely vital that we continue to support that principle, because if we abandon it we abandon parliament and the traditions of parliament. If we really want to reflect the opinion of every constituent, we can plug them all into a television set. Every bill in the House could be

voted upon by every eligible voter. That is quite feasible. Computers can do it but, quite frankly, parliamentary democracy would become irrelevant in that case-and I do not want to see parliamentary democracy become irrelevant.
As I have said, I think this argument deflects a meaningful discussion of the question of whether we have death or not in terms of the sanctions under our Criminal Code. What we have created in this society is tremendous disparities of income. Every study shows that in the urban areas, regardless of the general wealth, the greater the disparities, the higher the crime rate and the higher the murder rate. One could go to New York, Detroit, Vancouver or Montreal; this is consistent throughout the world. Expectations are raised and people are brain-damaged and manipulated by exposure to violence on the media. When you put these factors together, you clearly increase that risk.
I should like to turn, again, to the responsibility of the media, although I spoke about it at some length yesterday, Mr. Speaker. The time has passed when we should allow the media to peddle violence for the purpose of selling any product. I think that is wrong. We must give some attention to the effect that violence in the media is having. I should like to refer to an article which appeared in Monday's Globe and Mail which carried a report from Miami Beach. The article said:
A psychiatric research team reports that violence on television may produce similar behaviour on the part of the viewer.
The study, by three researchers at the University of California at Los Angeles, was presented here yesterday to the annual meeting of the American Psychiatric Association.
Dr. Roderic Gorney, associate professor of psychiatry and director of the study said that men assigned to watch only violent programs showed more hurtful behaviour in their homes than men who watched only programs regarded as helpful or pro-social.
The media have some responsibility, but they are not cleaning their own backyard. Mr. Speaker, I have known the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt) for a long time. She has taken a keen interest in all matters of crime, not merely the death penalty, and has dealt quite articulately with the case for retention. I should like to deal specifically with some of her arguments now. The hon. member indicated that the probability of mistake is minuscule, that the only known mistake is the Evans-Christie case in England. She is willing to admit that in that case an innocent man was hanged. I am sorry she is not here, because I should like to refresh her memory about a number of cases that she was involved in as a journalist.
When I was in law school, a man called Ducharme was accused of killing a woman. The prosecuting lawyer was Tom Norris, who later became Mr. Justice Norris, a judge of the Supreme Court and a judge of the Court of Appeal, and subsequently head of the Norris commission which was instrumental in cleaning up the Great Lakes in terms of related labour gangsterism. Mr. Norris has been an abolitionist for a long time and is an articulate spokesman for that side of the case. I am convinced that one of the reasons for his view is his involvement as prosecutor in the Ducharme case. There was no confession in that case, and while there was suspicion, there was never any hard or
May 26, 1976

conclusive evidence that Ducharme had in fact killed the 44-year old spinster. Although the circumstances were extremely suspicious and overwhelming enough for the jury to convict, I think everyone involved in that case had some real doubts.
Then we have the Coffin case, the Truscott case and the Raymond Cook case. We can read and read and read, Mr. Speaker-but how do we give a man back his life? How do we correct the awesome error the state makes when it takes the life of an innocent man? Yesterday the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) pointed out that the capacity for error is small-and I agree. There are a number of safety factors within the Criminal Code to guard against mistakes. But no justice system is perfect, and that is one of the reasons why so many people involved in it are abolitionists, why so many who are prosecutors, defenders of judges come down on the side of abolition. The circumstances and facts of every case vary. They know that there are many cases where they can be certain-but are they morally certain? I think before we take anyone's life we should be morally certain.
Some people say we should exclude the circumstantial case. To paraphrase the Hodges' rule, it says that circumstances have to be consistent with guilt and inconsistent with innocence. They forget that the question of identification of the murderer becomes a key part of any murder trial where there is a dispute about identification. If we exclude that, then we exclude almost every case in terms of the death penalty.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway dealt with the case of James Carey in which she was heavily involved. His is probably the living embodiment of a case for abolition. He continues to live in Fredericton, New Brunswick, and I believe was head of the Rotary Club. He has been an exemplary citizen since his release from penitentiary. He was charged with the murder of a police officer in Vancouver, and the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway was instrumental in having his death sentence commuted. I think all of society is in her debt for the work she did to*see that James Carey did not die.
The hon. member has justified the change in her position on capital punishment on the fact that Carey did not pull the trigger. But I want to ask her about the case of Miller and Cockrell who are presently awaiting the death penalty for the murder of a policeman in Cloverdale. One pulled the trigger, and the other did not. Is that a case where one sentence should be commuted but not the other? I do not believe we should commute the long prison sentences involved in that case; there should clearly be long sentences for that kind of despicable murder. But the death sentence in that case will not provide safety for the police officers of Canada. The death sentence would not have saved the life of the constable who was killed.
Some confusion in this debate arises from the belief that those who argue for retention argue for safety. I say they argue a case that will not stand in terms of deterrence, and will not stand in terms of providing additional public safety. In the history of man, the death penalty itself has never been applied in a non-discriminatory way. The prejudices of people, the politization of the penalty, mean that the underprivileged hang and the rich never hang.
Capital Punishment
That will be just as true if we return to the imposition of the death penalty in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I do not think my son, if he ever committed the crime of murder, which God forbid, would hang because of the political pressure that would be placed upon cabinet by the PTA and people who would have known his history, and so on. But if you take the case of a native child on a reserve who may kill, he would probably hang. That was the tradition in Canada, and certainly in the United States where 50 per cent of those hanged were black. They certainly did not commit 50 per cent of the murders in the United States. We have to ask ourselves some deep and searching questions about the way we apply the death penalty. The final decision belongs with the cabinet, Mr. Speaker, but we are all fallible and human. There is no way we can bring the death penalty back in Canada and apply it in a fair and consistent way. If we bring it back, we will be lowering the standards of justice in the country in a very significant way.
Yesterday the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta) referred to the problems faced by the people who have responsibility for guarding long-term prisoners who are also murderers. I have some sympathy for their position, Mr. Speaker. We know that a 25-year sentence is really a 15-year sentence in terms of this bill. I suspect that in almost every case, certainly the majority of cases, parole will be granted shortly after 15 years have been served, when the judicial report is made. If we argue that abolition of the death penalty creates a high risk for guards-and I admit there is some risk-we must concede there is also a high risk for police officers trying to apprehend someone when the death penalty is imposed for murder. In those circumstances, the felon has nothing to lose. That is why the death penalty was abolished in Austria, and indeed the police were instrumental in having it abolished. They felt it compromised their safety when apprehending dangerous criminals. I hope we will give serious attention to this view. I think it is important that we have hope and confidence in our fellowman.
When we do something which leads people to abandon hope and confidence, we take a backward step; we go opposite to the direction of social progress, opposite to the direction which leads to social improvement. When Wilber-force argued in the British House of Commons that slavery should be abolished, people thought he was crazy. After all, slavery had been with us since the dawn of history. His concept was revolutionary; but Wilberforce fought for his ideals and won, and his victory was a small step forward for man. When we abolish the death penalty, we shall take another faltering step forward, a faltering step which will lead to the long-term improvement of mankind. As a society, we must seek to become more humane, compassionate and civilized. Surely that is the end we seek.
I urge members of parliament to gird up their courage, to listen to their conscience and to abolish the death penalty.
I say, you will not increase the murder rate in Canada; you will enhance the safety of all Canadians.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill now before us expresses the will of this government to
955 68-43(4

May 26, 1976
Capital Punishment
abolish completely the death penalty as a possible punishment for the murder of a policeman or a prison guard.
The question is still very controversial and even if the bill were to be passed that would not necessarily mean the end of the debate; far from it, because the reasons for the discussions remain very active today despite the fact that, for several years now, the government has tried to decrease the application of the act as much as possible by gradually restricting its application and even simply refusing to apply it. Mr. Speaker, in fact one can say that the act was amended three times since 1961 at which time every murder was considered to be capital murder for which the penalty was always the death penalty.
In September of 1961, the act set up two categories: first, capital murder with the possible penalty of capital punishment. Here we were dealing with premeditated murder, that of a policeman, a prison guard or a judicial authority, and finally murders committed in the course of another criminal act. The second category included all other murders the penalty for which could be as severe as life imprisonment. Later, in September 1967, the act was amended again for a period of five years, reducing the notion of premedidated murder solely to those who were found guilty of the murder of representatives of the law.
In 1972, five years later, the House of Commons decided by a free vote that only the murder of a peace officer would be considered as capital murder. We know, Mr. Speaker, what happened afterwards, and we know very well that, for all practical purposes, it meant the abolition of capital punishment, since all death penalties have been commuted to life sentences for several years. This matter has been discussed for several years, yet it is still with us today.
I had the opportunity to take part in many debates on capital punishment both outside and in the House, where I first came in 1968. I heard practically every possible argument and figure from either side, and I personally quoted many of them to support my views and add weight to my arguments. In 1972, I even went as far as to conduct a survey of 18 heads of families in my riding, the results of which I submitted to the House to emphasize that the great majority of our fellow citizens were in favour of reinstating capital punishment, and it is still practically the same situation that prevails in the riding of Richmond which I have the honour to represent today in the House.
For instance, in February 1976, 1777 heads of families in my riding answered a question which I put to all of them. Question (A) was as follows: Do you agree that cabinet should commute death penalties to life sentences after the court has condemned the criminal to death? Out of a total of 1676 people who answered this question, 330 said "Yes", and 1,346 "No". Therefore, 19.7 per cent are in favour and 80.3 per cent are against. Question (B) was as follows: In the case of premeditated and capital murder, do you approve of the death penalty? Out of a total of 1,688 answers to this question, there were 1,469 "Yes" and 219 "No". Which means that 87 per cent are in favour, while 13 per cent are opposed to it. To question (C): Should parole be granted to a criminal convicted of premeditated murder, 1,676 people answered, 97 said "Yes", and 1,579 "No". This means that 5.8 per cent are in favour and 94.2 per cent are against.

Since the matter has again been brought in the House today, I intend this time to deal with it in a completely different way. This is why I will not refer to statistics and various views to discuss more particularly the basic principles involved as far as the death penalty is concerned. I want my intervention to be objective and clear of all emotivity or passion often raised during such discussions. First I will state the main points generally made for both sides of the matter. I then intend to put the death penalty in its present context where society is confronted with criminality, while recalling also how the penalty was applied throughout history. Afterwards, I would also like to interpret the policy of government authorities on the question and finally indicate my own position.
Should we be for or against the death penalty? This is the question. As to arguments made for the abolition or retention of capital punishment they are numerous and I will mention only the main ones. Those who wish at any cost to abolish entirely the death penalty sometimes say that it is merely a barbarian remnant which has no room in a so-called modern and civilized society. Some will advocate the humanitarian rehabilitation of murderers alleging the dignity of human life. Others will say that it is mere revenge, a backward application of the law of retaliation. Finally, a few, such as the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) for example, will argue that it is a useless step since, according to them, figures do not prove that it reduces the number of murders. Those are the major reasons advanced by those in favour of abolishing this penalty.
On the other hand, the retentionists suggest mainly that this is an effective means to reduce the number of murders by arousing the fear of punishment in the criminals. Others suggest that the carrying out of this sentence would be a deterrent for potential criminals. Finally, others say that the implementation of capital punishment would automatically deal with those who relapse into crime and commit more than one murder.
All those arguments from both sides may be discussed one by one and supported by figures and striking examples. I will return indirectly to this later on, but for the moment I would like to place this issue in its true context of everyday life and to relate it to our own society. I sincerely believe that only this way will we be able to deal with the issue realistically, because otherwise the discussion remains philosophical and I consider, if I may use that phrase, that it is only hot air which leads nowhere.
As a matter of fact, if we do not want to miss the point completely, we must agree at the outset that the problem of capital punishment is closely linked to several other social problems. Therefore, we cannot deal with it and analyze it without relating it to the other problems our society is afflicted with, because they are the other pieces of the puzzle of crime, of which murder is the last and most serious one. We must therefore criticize society as a whole if we are to understand the role capital punishment may or may not play. One must be completely blind not to admit that our modern society is faced with huge difficulties with regard to crime. And what becomes particularly alarming is that this phenomenon becomes general and affects all social strata.
May 26, 1976

To give a good description of the problem, let us say that there are two kinds of crimes: flagrant crimes and discrete crimes. Among flagrant crimes there may be various types of thefts (housebreaking, simple theft, car theft, robbery) as well as assault and battery, rape and, finally, murder. On the other hand, among the so-called discrete crimes, there are a great number of actions that are sometimes very surprising on the part of quite ordinary people which nobody would consider as reprehensible actions. Nevertheless, we may put in this category all kinds of tax evasions, secret stock exchange transactions, bribes, time stolen by an employee idle at work, and lies.
To convince oneself of the gravity of the situation, one just has to consider the worth of a promise in today's world, where even a signed contract is not honoured any more. Even if it seems a very strange thing to say, crime is almost accepted socially as something which is not quite bad or wrong.
That is why it is not unusual to hear people boast about the way they have financially deceived a partner, an employer or someone else, as though it were an achievement. Unfortunately, this way of thinking has been spreading on a large scale during the last few years and has literally poisoned human relationships in the financial, social and domestic fields. It is thus that we have progressively destroyed honesty, a sense of honour and trust to make way for this new type of morality which is actually nothing more than the resurgence of the law of the jungle under which each individual tries to grab all he can get without offering anything in return. If carried to the extreme, this goes as far as the elimination of the other individual, and there we have the whole process of crime which is almost accepted today and ranges from mere lie to murder. And this social acceptance of crime is emphasized even more by advertising which, generally speaking, pictures various offences under a glamourous guise and even turns some criminals into international stars. I shall go even further and suggest that our laws treat criminals better than they treat the honest silent majority of people.
To be convinced, one only has to see how considerate we are about providing sports facilities, entertainment and weekend passes for the criminal, whereas the jobless father has to fight with the unemployment insurance office to get the cheque he is lawfully entitled to. We are thinking of giving a salary to prisoners, but because of the anti-inflation program we reject higher family allowances and so on. One may notice in all this that the victims are forgotten and that he who is against this new morale is not even considered as up-to-date or normal. This brings me to say that the present debate is biased, because generally our laws as well as society itself already favour the criminal. I would go as far as saying that the present discussions are basically false; as evidence, one only has to recall how senior employees of the department succeeded in bringing the minister to sell the idea of abolishing capital punishment by reducing it gradually these last years.
The other question which arises, Mr. Speaker, is this: Is justice capable of being just? Before going any further on capital punishment as such, I wish to ask a question which, in my view, is fundamental and which has not been mentioned by anyone or very few people. Can justice as we know it today be trusted and is it capable of applying
Capital Punishment
effectively and fairly laws such as the one on capital punishment? This question is extremely important since it must be expected that those who are responsible for administering justice practice what they preach, so that the whole of society is trustful and their work is fruitful.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, the answer is not completely reassuring. Unfortunately, one must see reality as it is, and integrity seems to be gradually stepping aside to be replaced by bribery, political dealings, patronage and all those types of new ethics which creep into large corporations, governments and even justice. One only has to see how certain judges are appointed, sometimes more for their political services than their integrity.
The death penalty is not something new and history tells us that it has been applied through times in every possible way and for all imaginable purposes. In the beginning of mankind, millions of men, women and even children were executed; in ancient times, for instance, criminals were done away through stoning, hanging and crucifying. In ancient Rome, they were thrown to the lions and throughout the medieval period, in the name of religion we burned, quartered and beheaded those who were called heretics.
Then the guillotine appeared in France. After came the electric chair in the United States as well as the gas chamber. Those were the ways to apply capital punishment but there were also other means; during the Second World War, Hitler's Germany condemned to death millions of human beings-Polish, Ukrainians, Jews and others-who were hanged, shot or passed through the gas chamber. The death penalty in those days was called Dachau, Auschwitz and so on.
Closer to us, Vietnam has been the scene of numerous executions under the cover of the raging war. Quite recently again, according to the media, capital punishment was imposed in Angola on several people unwilling to help the UNITA, and I can well imagine that it was the same with ALNF and ALPM. To be convinced, one only has to recall the recent piece of news indicating that in northern Angola every woman was raped at least three times by Cuban soldiers. We can then understand why the death penalty may be imposed for whatever reason in some countries.
Yet that is only a very brief historical account on capital punishment, but I think it is sufficient to realize all the abuses to which this penalty gave rise from the beginnings of humanity until today. If I take the trouble of raising all these facts on the death penalty, it is to place the issue in its context. Closer to us, Mr. Speaker, let us see what are the attitudes of governments and ministers responsible for that issue. Last year, the chiefs of police in the province of Quebec, meeting in a convention, adopted one resolution as did the Canadian association of mayors, urging the government to impose capital punishment in view of the incredible increase in violence and in the number of murders.
In reply to a question, the Solicitor General (Mr. All-mand) later stated:
I categorically refuse to be associated in any way with a hanging.
That is his privilege. On the other hand, the then minister of justice of the province of Quebec, Mr. Jerome Cho-quette, stated he disagreed with that resolution and the

May 26, 1976
Capital Punishment
death penalty was not consistent with the concept of human progress. That is serious. If someone in the street had made such a suggestion, there would not have been great harm. But when one or two ministers responsible for supporting and enforcing the law will not enforce it or respect it themselves, it is getting serious. Is that the so-called progress concept? Is that the kind of attitude public authorities should have to instill respect for the law? In such circumstances, how can they require citizens to abide by the income tax act, for instance, or any other act for that matter? Maybe that is one of the links in the heavy chain of crime that is crushing society at all levels.
Mr. Speaker, some people refer to the Bible to defend their theory on capital punishment or in support of this legislation. As far as the Solicitor General is concerned, I wish he had been as energetic to enforce the law as it now stands as he has been in selling his or his officials' idea of complete abolition. He spoke on the subject on a number of occasions and I shall refer to the speech he made in March 1975 entitled: Prevention and control of violent crime in Canada. At some point, he referred once again to the Bible forbidding to kill. That point is made now and then, and it deserves closer examination.
The Solicitor General stated, and I quote:
The paramount issue is one of morality. Are we justified in taking a human life through capital punishment? Execution does not erase the crime of murder. It takes away another life. The commandment, "Thou shalt not kill" is part of our Judaeo-Christian heritage. It emphasizes the value of human life.
True, the Lord gave that law. It is also a fact that this same law stresses the paramount importance of human life. But it is not quite fair to use that one verse out of context and without any reference to the other directions God gave us, in an attempt to prove He is against capital punishment. That would go against what the Bible says further on. First of all, God created man free, so that he may accept or reject the commandments He gave him to be happy. Now, man misused that freedom by rejecting the divine commandments, preferring to decide by himself what is good or wrong, and we know with what result which was not long coming, since the first generation had its first murderer, Cain.
So, in the beginning, seeing that man misused his freedom and rejected even His commandments, the Creator determined penalties according to offences, and that is why God said, as reported in the Bible, and I quote:
Whoever sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed.
That is quite different from what the Solicitor General said.
Mr. Speaker, in the same address, the Solicitor General proposed a whole series of preventive measures, and I quote:
What, then, do I suggest in place of this? Some of the measures that I propose to prevent and reduce crime are the following: better trained, better deployed and better equipped policemen; effective gun control, proactive rather than reactive police work, more effective correctional programs for juveniles and adults ... and so on . ..
Mr. Speaker, I want to stress that those are truly fantastic proposals and the minister must be commended for them.
The only thing I regret is that those are very nice words to put on a postcard, for instance, but apart from that, they

are nearly useless since they do not correspond at all to reality. They are more like smoke than anything else. I have the impression that the minister is still thinking like a Pee-Wee and that he has been drafted by the major leagues without realizing it.
Professional criminals and organized crime are omnipotent and some people even say that they have friends quite near the government... Gangland murders are becoming more and more frequent, and so are senseless murders. The streets of our major cities are no longer safe. Violence increases everywhere. Our "modern and sophisticated" civilization has become that of highjacking, political assassination, hostage taking and kidnapping. Even our youths take part in this spiral of violence and seem to prepare a society which will be far from restful.
For instance, the United States News and World Report issue of January 26 last published an especially impressive article entitled "Terror in Schools". It says that violence and vandalism have taken epidemic proportions to which no one seems able to remedy. Between 1970 and 1973, murders in schools increased by 18 per cent, theft by 37 per cent, assaults on students by 85 per cent and assaults on teachers by 77 per cent. Indeed, in view of the urgent need to put a stop to violence, the Attorney General of the United States, Mr. Edward Levi, who had been against this penalty before, is now in favour of capital punishment in certain cases.
During this time, the Solicitor General intends to aim his action nearly exclusively at prevention, as if this were sufficient. This is very naive reasoning! I believe there must be prevention, but it is not enough; as in the education of children, it is necessary to have just but strict penalties according to the seriousness of the offence. Whether we accept this or not, it is a deterrent which, to some extent, will stop certain criminals. Mr. Speaker, these last few years, we have forgotten the victims.
Our justice has become so slow and lax that we forget about the victims and we even go as far as considering it horrible to punish criminals for the simple reason that too much time has elapsed between the crime and judgement or the carrying out of the judgement so that it is hard to see why they are punished. In this sense, the death penalty has long become ridiculous because of a simple political game.
As I have already said, to be efficient, a judgement must be carried out. Even if it is in the Criminal Code, that is not enough. It must be carried out immediately after the judgement and it should not be delayed by never ending time lapses, until the crime if forgotten or until it seems almost innocuous. Otherwise, the criminals are finally considered as victims, as this bill wishes and we forget about the true victims. Besides, I would like, Mr. Speaker, to read to the House a letter written on February 8 this year, which I have just received, and which tells a lot about this subject:
Dear Mr. Beaudoin:
I send this letter to you and to anyone who might be interested in this subject. The results of the present discussions about the death penalty affect the whole country. A bill to abolish the death penalty will be introduced in the House on February 9, 1976. This is a rather curious coincidence but for me this particular date is the saddest of all. You see, sir, February 9 is the date of my daughter's birthday. She would have been 17 this year but she will never be. My daughter Sharron was
May 26, 1976

savagely killed on March 29, 1975. She had gone to see some friends four blocks from where we live but never got there. Three days later, her body was discovered in a field a few miles away. She had been kept prisoner for three days, raped, hit so hard that she had a double jaw fracture, a skull fracture, a broken nose and ripped organs.
The cause of death: asphyxia by blood in her lungs and her abductor also strangled her. She had been bound and gagged. In looking at statistics about murder in recent years, I must say there has been a very steep increase in the number of murders. As an example, in the province of Quebec alone, there were 17 murders in 1955, 53 in 1965, 217 in 1975. Something has to be done.
Not only is the number of murders increasing dangerously, but also the nature of the crime is becoming ever more sadistic. With the laws as they now stand. I have to believe in capital punishment, not neccessari-ly by hanging or by the electric chair, but by sleep, the same way we put a dangerous dog to sleep. As to the argument about the risk of putting innocents to death it would be the exceptions who would remain in prison until they are recognized innocent. In my view, the law is a joke. At present, capital punishment for the murder of a policeman or prison guard exists, but only in the texts of law and not in reality. If you cannot trust the law, whom can you trust? I believe in God and I consider myself a Christian and I believe in the word of God when he speaks to Moses in the Bible in Numbers, chapter 35, verses 16 to 21. Those assassins eat, sleep, play cards, tell jokes, have a lot of fun and now they want to form an association in prisons while their innocent victims who had their lives taken away lie in their coffins.
Those victims cannot speak for themselves.
They need your vote.
I trust in God to help you.
Mrs. Yvonne Prior 445 Congregation Street Montreal.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, in the present state of things where reality indicates a frightening increase in murders and violence in general, continuing to spare hard-core murderers, as proposed in the bill before us, is automatically to condemn others, that is innocents, to pay the price with their lives. So under this legislation the government and particularly the Solicitor General indicate that they want first to protect criminals by reducing their sentences-pending the time when they will offer them trophies and trips to the South-rather than protect the citizens.
Not only must I be against this bill but I must say that in my opinion a responsible government should immediately reinstate capital punishment in Canada, and I should be actually enforced in cases of capital murder-I stress capital-premeditated or committed in the perpetration of another criminal act. However, I expressed certain reservations and that is why I pointed out certain abuses that had resulted from the death penalty in history. I also think that the death penalty alone will not solve the problem of murder because murder represents only the last link in the whole chain of crime which should also be reduced by other means.
However, I know it would check the increase of all types of murders. But I also know that the Solicitor General, as well as the government, wants his legislation to pass at all costs with what is, I hope, nothing but touching guilelessness. I for one took the time to consider all the basic principles of that issue. As for the rest, the Solicitor General, supported to some extent by the cabinet and his caucus, will have to assume the responsibility of the view he defends so desperately. Mr. Speaker, in conclusion, I wish to quote a few sentences spoken on April 21, 1968, at Notre-Dame de Paris by Reverend Marcel Cornells, on the
Capital Punishment
53rd anniversary of the mass murders of Armenians. This reverend father said, and I agree whole heartedly:
Each time we remain unconcerned or shed hypocritical tears in the presence of crime, an even more serious crime is about to be committed, a crime for which we shall no doubt assume our share of responsibility.
He who through his passivity and unconcern is an accessory to a crime committed today is already an accessory to the more serious crime which will be committed tomorrow, and let him beware because he who is now only an indifferent spectator could become tomorrow a bleeding victim.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to start by congratulating the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt). I have attended the House and listened to a good deal of the debate on this very important and emotional issue, and I thought he was one of very few members who brought some new thoughts and new approaches to this over-all problem. Were he in the House, I would congratulate him.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
