speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Unlike some of the members of this chamber who have been here for some years, this is the first occasion I have had to address the House on the subject of capital punishment. Since the time I was elected to parliament I do not believe I have dealt with any issue that has been more sensitive or more difficult in coming to a conclusion. I think I can say in all truthfulness that I have approached this subject with an open mind. I did not have any great depth of knowledge of the law when I originally analysed this problem, and I sincerely felt I could be persuaded by arguments for either side. I wanted to maintain an objective perspective on capital punishment because I considered it my duty to evaluate all reasonable arguments on both sides of question. It is my respectful submission that members of this House who have prepared themselves as either ardent abolitionists or ardent reten-tionists have seriously limited their capabilities of giving their constituents' arguments a fair hearing.
Because I am not a lawyer I did not have a full grasp of the legal intricacies of the question. I should like to express my indebtedness to Senator Neiman, of the other place, whose excellent speech of May 29, 1975, illuminates the salient legal issues of the capital punishment question, and I recommend it to all hon. members to read.
I have, personally, made every attempt to research the capital punishment question thoroughly. I have spoken with lawyers, policemen, criminologists and social workers. Indeed, I have had the opportunity of discussing the issues with people who have spent a considerable number of years on death row. For the benefit of my constituents and for my own discipline in preparing for this vote coming up, I have written papers on the history of capital punishment, on the law on capital punishment and on the referendum on capital punishment. In addition to that, I have distributed to a good number of people a number of papers, particularly one on theology and capital punishment.
The greatest part of my study was devoted to discussing this subject with my constituents. Like most members, the correspondence I have received on the subject has been voluminous. The topic arose at the two latest series of town

Capital Punishment
hall meetings recently held in my riding, and I certainly gained a great amount of valuable information from my constituents on those occasions.
Like all Canadians, the people of Peel-Dufferin-Simcoe have a deep-rooted concern about the direction our criminal justice system is heading. They are concerned that society may not adequately be protected against violent crime. They want reassurances that our legal institutions are capable of dealing with anti-social elements properly and effectively. A sense of anxiety or uneasiness has naturally followed the wave of violent crime of recent years which has taken unprecedented sensational dimensions. Through radio and television, Canadians are intimate witnesses to such incredible international incidents as the recent murders of diplomats in Paris, and each day on the news we hear about the incessant, senseless violence that troubles Northern Ireland. Disturbing incidents of this nature cannot help but exert an unsettling influence on our own feeling of security here in Canada.
Here at home many Canadians perceive that violent crime is spiralling out of control. The truth is that we enjoy one of the safest societies in the world. To a large extent, this distorted perception of violent crime has been fostered by the media's sensational treatment of isolated incidents such as gangland murders in Montreal and hostage incidents in British Columbia prisons. We often hear the viewpoint that criminals in Canada are conducting their nefarious activities without any fear of restraint or apprehension. I do not believe this reflects reality. If it were true, Canada would by now have fallen into the same hopeless state of anarchy and confusion which engulfs more and more nations.
This is not to say that various aspects of our criminal law process are not in desperate need of reform. People are genuinely concerned about the shortcomings in our system of granting bail, and I am glad to see the provisions of Bill C-71 have now been proclaimed into law. This legislation should make strides in reducing the abuses which our bail laws have suffered in the past.
The vast majority of Canadians are disturbed about the proliferation of guns in our society and their increasing use in criminal acts. Part of Bill C-83 seeks to redress this problem, and as I have spoken on this matter on two earlier occasions in the House I will not deal with it further today. There is concern about the parole system in Canada, about the process of temporary release of inmates convicted of dangerous offences, and about the sentencing procedures for dealing with incorrigible offenders; but Bill C-83 attempts to respond to these problems also. The peace and security proposals before parliament are, again, the kind of action many Canadians are demanding. They are anxious to see effective measures placed into law which hold a promise of combating the trend toward violent crime.
I should like to put this in better perspective. What is the question with which we are dealing? I do not believe we are dealing in isolation with the question: Are members in favour of capital punishment or not? Or, on a theoretical basis, whether or not they are in favour of capital punishment. If that were the case, certainly I would think that the polls are correct in that 70 per cent to 75 per cent of
[Mr. Milne.l
Canadians favour the retention of capital punishment under these conditions.
Surely, the question parliament is considering at this point in time and, indeed, will be voting on in perhaps not too many days, is the following: Given better law and order through the provisions of the peace and security bill, such as gun control, sentencing of dangerous offenders, wiretapping, crime inquiries, parole, bail as passed recently, crime prevention and redefinition of murder, with first-degree murder carrying a life sentence of 25 years, certainly before parole can even be applied for, do we still need capital punishment on the law books of Canada to deal effectively with crime in our society?
With respect, Mr. Speaker, may I say that I think that is very different from the question: Are we, or are we not, in favour of capital punishment? This is the difficulty I have with public opinion polls. I do not think they accurately reflect on the question with which parliament is dealing, because most of the polls I have seen which have given this preponderance of opinion on the retentionist side have asked the simple question concerning whether or not we are simply in favour of capital punishment.
My experience with town hall meetings, which I should like to share with the House, has been that when the question of capital punishment has come up, it is true that when a poll is taken often 75 per cent of the people attending are in favour of capital punishment. But on a review of the law, the royal prerogative, the plea of clemency and the history of the law as it has been developed, and after discussing the provisions of Bill C-83 and then asking how many people are still in favour of capital punishment, the result is very evenly divided. In fact, we have had meetings at which perhaps only one-third of those present, with a better understanding of the law, would still want capital punishment retained.
I think, as many members have mentioned, that is reflected in the Gallup poll as published in the Ottawa Citizen of March 4, to the effect that what society wants is better law and order and that it may be satisfied with that instead of capital punishment. The question is asked: If we can achieve better law and order, would we, or would we not, be satisfied to see an end to the death penalty in Canada? I really think that is the question. The national poll indicated that 48 per cent would say yes, that 48 per cent would say no, and that the other 4 per cent are not sure. I would point out to hon. members that should this bill fail to pass and we return to capital punishment and carry out capital punishment with the three people on death row on July 15, I really suspect there would be a very different feeling across Canada and I would think that a poll taken at that time would indicate that a very small percentage of the people would in fact support capital punishment.
There is one other aspect of this on which I want to comment because I think it is rather important. I refer to the question of the numbers. In 1974 there were something like 545 murders in Canada. Only seven of these involved policemen or prison guards. If the law had been applied systematically, I wonder if we would have had seven cases of capital punishment. One thing that is disappointing to
May 26, 1976

me is why in this House we are not debating more seriously the question of the 538 other murders. Surely they should be of equal importance and should share a good deal of the time of the House. I think this is what the hon. member for New Westminster devoted most of his speech to.
I have been reading that some 70 per cent of the people who have been murdered have been known to the person committing the murder, and that probably 40 per cent of all these murders, which is well over 200, are domestic murders. It would seem to me that the time of the House would be well taken in a good discussion of some of the trends in our society which lead to the rapid increase in murder in domestic situations. I think of such things as our rapid trend toward urbanization, the poverty levels we have in certain areas, versus the expectation certain people have, the display of violence by the media on television, and so on, and such things as job frustration, overuse of alcohol, depression and drugs. I think members really should be talking about all these things, because in the case of prison guards and policemen we are dealing with something like half of 1 per cent of the crime and we are dealing with a very small percentage of the murders committed in Canada.
It seems to me that in coming to a conclusion on this very difficult question there are three major considerations. One is the revenge approach. There is the question of is, or is not, capital punishment a deterrent, and whether or not we really are interested in rehabilitation of people who commit crimes. I might just comment on revenge. It certainly is an opinion held by many people: they equate revenge with justice. A high percentage of the mail I have received merely supports capital punishment on this basis. I have great difficulty with that.
The law has developed over the years. Members will know, as well as I do, that we have hanged over 700 people during the history of Canada. The first person to be hanged, I understand, was a 15-year old girl, for the crime of stealing. Surely, the law and our society have developed a good deal since that point in time, who committed the offence is concerned. I really think that in this debate we would be wrong not to talk about some of the needs for rehabilitation and the reform of our penal institutions, because as an alternative to capital punishment, if we are to commit murderers to prison for terms of 25 years, we cannot neglect our present responsibility to modernize the prison system and provide work and rehabilitation situations in order to prevent the further development of a potentially violent and destructive malaise among our prison population.
Surely, it is socially unconscionable and irresponsible to imprison a murderer or any offender for practically indefinite periods of time without seriously evaluating the environment to which they will be subjected. It is of no benefit to society to throw away the key and by doing so increase the volatility and inhumanity of the prison setting. I think a policy of longer prison terms must be accompanied, not by a superficial satisfaction that greater justice has been done, but by an augmented concern for the treatment of the prisoner over these longer periods of time. Really, the key question is whether or not capital punishment is a deterrent to others who might commit murder.
Capital Punishment
My research-and I would like to think that I have done as much as any member of this House-cannot substantiate that it is a deterrent to other people who might commit crime, at least this type of crime. Certainly, if there is some question concerning whether or not it is a deterrent, it would seem to me that the responsibility really should be on those who support the retentionist stand to prove how strong a deterrent it is in fact.
I have reviewed, as I am sure have many others, the experience in other countries. I think Italy and France are two countries which might be compared. In Italy, which is an abolitionist country, the murder rate is 3.21 per 100,000, compared to France, which is a retentionist country, with a rate of 5.11 murders per 100,000. When we look at the statistical evidence in the United States there is very little difference in the murder rate between bordering states which have or which do not have capital punishment. I think, in reviewing this, we might refer to a few statements made by people who have looked into the matter in great detail. In 1958, the Massachusetts special committee investigating the abolition of the death penalty concluded:
There appears to be, in fact, no greater deterrent effect in capital punishment than in a sentence of life. It does not contribute to the reduction of murder, it is simply an easy and harmful way of satisfying the need "to do something about it".
In Great Britain, the royal commission on capital punishment, which held hearings on the subject from 1949 to 1953, reported:
The general conclusion which we have reached is that there is no clear evidence in any of the figures we have examined that the abolition of capital punishment has led to an increase in the homicide rate or that its reintroduction has led to a fall.
I fully concur with Schusessler in his report entitled "Murder and the Death Penalty" that statistical studies have uniformly concluded that the death penalty is consequential as a deterrent and that the relative frequency of murder in a given population is a function of the cultural conditions. So the basic point is: does capital punishment deter anyone from committing murder more than the prospect of life imprisonment? Professor Wilson says, as quoted in the minister's opening speech:
It is a matter of dispute whether any penalty will have a deterrent effect on murders, but surely the prospect of a long prison term will have as much as most others.
I support that point of view quite strongly. There are a couple of other arguments that 1 would like to put forward. There seems to be a strong viewpoint that if we were to hang one, two or more people, that would effectively control crime in our society. I do not believe that and I do not subscribe to it. I oppose that point of view, because surely members who have been studying Bill C-83 carefully and the background to it would see in the statistics that the explosion of crime is really at the lower end of the crime scale. Crimes of violence as a percentage of both total and Criminal Code offences have not changed over the last 10 or 12 years. If anything, as a percentage there are less of them today than there were 10 years ago. What we are dealing with is a rapidly increasing rate of armed robberies, of arson, of sexual offences, of assault, and so on. There are more murders within the domestic setting. I do not think that if on July 15 we decide to hang two or three
13868

May 26, 1976
Capital Punishment
people, that will effectively control crime and there will no longer be any more corner milk stores robbed.
I am impressed with a quote from the Church Council of Justice and Corrections which reads as follows. I assume all hon. members have received material from them, but I would like to quote the following sentence:
The available evidence suggest that the sanction of capital punishment does not really promote public safety by deterring potential killers, but that it does engender a false security in the public mind, which in turns delays community and government efforts to seek creative, realistic and humane alternatives more likely to prevent violence and restrain the violent.
I would recommend this material to hon. members, particularly the point of view that is set down there. The other argument which I would like to put forward and which I think is relevant here is respect for the law. All members of the House have been receiving in their mail letters which show that the country is demanding a return to real, tough law and order to combat a perceived rise in violent crime. A great deal of concern focuses on the administration of laws which already exist, and there is a feeling that our courts and prosecutors are being too lenient with dangerous offenders.
It is important in this debate that the citizens of Canada be reminded of the dichotemy of the justice system provided under our constitution. Simply put, the federal government enacts the laws and the provinces are charged with their administration from the arrest stage through the prosecution and sentencing stages in our courts. It is my opinion that the large degree of public concern should be directed at the provincial attorneys general who have the responsibility of directing the administration of criminal justice in Canada. Many of our present laws provide our courts with sufficient latitude to dispose of cases involving public safety in a way that conforms with public opinion. But our courts have been reluctant to administer the present laws to their full extent. I submit that if we were to make the law so tough or to revert to laws which existed back in the eighteenth century, as many people are demanding, many people would not respect the law and I do not think the courts would administer such a law, nor do I think the police would police the law if we were to do that. I think we want to be a little careful in how tough we make the law in response to many people who are demanding a return to the law which existed at the turn of the century.
In the remaining few minutes I have, I want to touch briefly on two other points. I want to speak as have many other members, about the concern I have about an individual who might be convicted of committing first-degree murder receiving a fair trial. I would not have thought this issue to be so important a year and half or two years ago, but I do today. Surely, all hon. members are conscious of the attitude being displayed toward minority groups here in this country recently and even, in fact, toward some language groups. That is why I raise this question of whether a fair trial can be held, because when we talk about the state taking the life of a human being we must have absolute confidence that the state can guarantee consistently fair trials with the minimum possibility of error, and I am not sure that is possible.
Let us consider, as an example, a wealthy person who is very articulate, well dressed, can afford the very best
[Mr. Milne.1
lawyer and witnesses brought from anywhere around the globe. The perception of that person by a jury, as compared to their perception of someone who may have considerable difficulty with the language, may not be articulate or well dressed and cannot afford the best legal support or witnesses, would be very different. I have heard lawyers discussing this in relation to the law courts. A businessman driving a very expensive car, who has had a few drinks at lunch, gets picked up by the police. Is he not treated quite differently from a youth with long hair, in a rusty old car who is charged with the same offence? There is a question as to whether in fact these two people are judged exactly the same in court. The U.S. Supreme Court has ruled capital punishment to be unconstitutional on these grounds.
We have to take into account that this is not an easy time to deal with the subject of capital punishment, given the present backlash with regard to minority groups, to those living in poverty, and, as I said, even to some linguistic groups. There is an old saying which applies here, that it is difficult to get a rich man into heaven and it is probably impossible to get his head into a noose. On the basis of religion, again, many people hold deep convictions on both sides of the issue, using religion as the basis of their viewpoint. Perhaps half the mail I have received is written from a religious point of view, and the same applies to people who have spoken to me on this subject. In fact I have in my files-and if time permitted I would even read them into the record-two excellent letters I have received from ministers in my riding, each minister representing a different church located across the road from each other. Both letters are excellent, well referenced and written with feeling and conviction. Each of them takes exactly the opposite point of view.
I respect these opinions completely using, as they do, religion as their basis. I only want to say that some people take a pretty narrow view by using a tew words from biblical writings to support their argument. I suggest that people should look at how the law changed from the early biblical times to later times and how the attitude toward the law changed over that period. I came across an excellent paper, in my view, entitled "Theology and Capital Punishment". It was written by a very learned scholar, and I recommend that hon. members read it. I found it most useful in responding to people with this viewpoint.
In summary, I do not challenge the right of the state to take a life. In fact, I found little fault and was relatively comfortable with the present law and how it was handled; in other words, that capital punishment is on the books but very rarely, if ever, carried out. In fact, in Canada it has not been carried out since 1962, but the law has been there in case some very extreme case should happen to warrant capital punishment. Like the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan), I would not be opposed to capital punishment for anyone who committed a second murder, either in or out of prison. My only apprehension in this whole question is about the security of prison guards, and so on. As a matter of fact, I thought about proposing this amendment myself at one time, and if the bill goes to committee-which I hope it will-and comes back with this amendment, I would most certainly support it.
May 26, 1976

However, I just cannot support capital punishment on a routine basis for every case either under the law as it is now written or for all first-degree murders, as recommended by many people and some hon. members of this House. That is why I will certainly support Bill C-84. The debate really boils down to the question of removing capital punishment from our Criminal Code or of practicing it on a systematic basis. These questions must be evaluated within the context of the facts which, in my opinion, show that capital punishment is not a significant deterrent to murder and that the mandatory use of capital punishment might well result in less possibility of punishing murderers, in view of the hesitation of juries to convict for capital murder. A couple of hon. members commented on that point this afternoon.
I believe very strongly that the death penalty creates the false expectation that we will reduce the amount of violence in our society. I suggest that the reverse is true, and that using murder or violence by the state to control violence would be neither an effective nor a desirable way of producing peace and security in Canada.
Having researched the subject carefully, given it much thought and shared many evenings with my constituents discussing this, and corresponding with them, I will certainly vote to support Bill C-84, Bill C-83 and any reasonable amendments which might appear when they come back from committee.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I enter this debate with a sense of having been here before, because I was in parliament in 1966 when the resolution on abolishing capital punishment was debated in this House. At that time there was a free vote, the freest vote this House has ever had and far freer than the one which is shaping up now. We debated the concept and not the legislation, and the concept of abolition was lost in that vote. The vote was followed by subsequent legislation, which is the legislation on the books now. The legislation which was brought in at that time was bad law, but it did something which was even more reprehensible; it ignored the free vote of parliament. I recall the debate which took place a little later on the legislation, when virtually all the debate which had taken place on the resolution was repeated. As it got down to the wire, I remember that it was a little doubtful whether that bill would pass.
At that time I was approached by a member of the NDP behind the curtain and asked how I was going to vote on the bill to limit capital punishment to the slayers of police officers and prison guards. I said I was going to vote against it. He expressed amazement and asked how I could vote against it. He pointed out that I had voted for abolition, and I replied that it was not an abolition bill. He said, "Yes, but you know they will commute them all". I knew, he knew, and I suspect that the government knew that it would commute them all and that what had been achieved was a kind of abolition but not, in a sense, by a vote in parliament.
I know that there were hon. members on both sides of the House who voted for that bill saying to themselves that at least in this instance the death penalty would be carried out, and I know that a great majority of the public accepted the bill which was presented in that light. It is from that shift and from the fact that the commutations have
Capital Punishment
been virtually automatic that a truly appalling situation has developed in this country in which there is now little faith in the law-making of this institution. We hear demands for national referendums because of the sense of frustration which has built up. We know that the government has come to an appalling point. I knew this would develop. It was only a matter of time after passing the legislation that the government would be faced with the terrible choice between mass commutation for all those people on death row, which is not politically acceptable, or mass execution, which is something very foreign to this country.
Then the government has compounded that problem one step further by offering abolition as a trade-off for gun control, or gun control as a trade-off for abolition, in a sense offering the public gun control in exchange for abolition. The people who own guns know that that is not a gift, but that it will be charged against them. It is not much wonder that the public is frustrated and that we in parliament find ourselves in this difficult situation.
As a person who voted for abolition then, and who is convinced now that the only sensible course for this parliament is to abolish capital punishment by a vote of parliament, I know that I probably go against a majority of my constituents, although that has not been accurately assessed, and I defy a great many of the simple polls which have been taken as representing accurate assessments of the will of the total constituency or, for that matter, the nation. Nevertheless, they create a sensitive, difficult problem and tension between members of parliament and constituents which should not be necessary. Abolition should come by a vote of this institution, and it must still be argued by the people who believe in abolition.
I did not blame police officers for wanting to broaden the grounds for capital punishment because the legislation which was passed singled them out in a way which was cruel. The other group, prison guards, are not visible to the public, but police officers are, and they have been the only visible people whose murder fell into a different class. That has concentrated attention on them which has not been in their best interests, and certainly the potential threat of the death penalty has not served to prevent their murder, either.
I deny the deterrent value of the death penalty, but the very singling out of those two groups in the legislation ascribed to the death penalty a deterrent value it did not have. Hon. members accepted the bill and voted for it because they felt they were protecting the people they wanted to protect. Here, again, the frustration of the commutations has compounded the intensity of feeling which has developed in the public. I still argue that it has been many, many years in this country, if ever, since life was forfeited for a life in murder. Our system of justice does not, and has not, rested on that delicate balance of a life for a life, although we have heard from all sides that it does and that if we do not maintain this balance, somehow the very structure of our system of justice will crumble under us. I do not believe that. It is easier to reply on a coupon in one of the advertisements run in the newspapers than it is to sit on a jury, as people still must, in our judicial system and after listening to the evidence, decide what the verdict should be. I find that juries have not changed since the one
95 568-44/4

May 26, 1976
Capital Punishment
about 1947 which refused to convict a murderer of two people very close to the community in which I had lived. I have not had much faith in the death penalty since that time, Mr. Speaker. My basic argument against it is its terrible unfairness.
In the Okanagan Valley, in the last year, there have been four cases of murder reduced to manslaughter, for which the sentences ranged from four to seven years. There was the case of the Crown v. Brown for the murder of Sadie Edwards at Sicamous. That case did not go to the jury because plea bargaining entered into it. There was a plea of guilty and a sentence of seven years was imposed for that murder. During the Christmas season, Sophie Loria West was charged with murder in the death of Earl Edward Walker. The circumstances of that murder fitted the very circumstances that so many people argue should lead to the gallows. It was murder for gain. There was a jury trial but, again, the charge was reduced to manslaughter and the sentence was four years. I have not had a single letter of protest from my constituency about any of these cases, Mr. Speaker. One was in my constituency, and the Walker case was just outside. There have been no letters of protest, so it would seem that the verdicts were acccepted.
Mr. Speaker, I am not convinced that a jury that would not convict on a charge of murder in a case which would carry life imprisonment would have the heart to convict in a case where the penalty was death, or that anything would have been changed in any of these cases if we had returned to the death penalty two years ago or in 1973 when this House last debated the subject.
I have talked to my constituents on this topic since 1966 and I find that everyone makes exceptions, everyone names categories of murderers that should not go to the gallows. Some tell me that I would change my mind if I came home one night and found my wife lying in a pool of blood on the kitchen floor. I reply that I do not know how I would act in a moment of such extreme emotion and tension. Then I ask them, how they can be sure that the murderer would hang? I know he would not if he were wealthy or influential-and that point has been dealt with before. He would not if he were young and caught the sympathy of the jury. He would not if he were insane and judged not fit to stand trial. He would not if he were drunk at the time and this lowered his ability to reason. And she would not if she were a woman. It is many years since a woman was hanged in this country. Very rarely, in English-speaking Canada, have we hanged a woman. They are the great exception.
I would point out that if I had committed the murder myself and called it a crime of passion-that other great excuse for murder that still runs through the domestic life of this country and treats the wife as a piece of property to be disposed of by the husband-I probably would not hang. Mr. Speaker, in my experience in this country, life has not been forfeit for life taken in every case.
Those people who send in the coupons in the newspaper advertisements are not asking for the death penalty as the law states it should be applied, or a simple broadening of it; over and over again they are asking for the death penalty without exception. I have written to some of them

and told them that 1 do not believe they really mean the death penalty without exception. I find that everybody has an exception. When we had capital punishment, in the end it involved hanging very few people. They had to be poor, old, ugly and male before they went to the gallows.
I should like to say a word to the abolitionists, Mr. Speaker, because I feel they have been strangely quiet in this debate. This is no time for silence. Although the argument may be tougher now, and although they will be up against a determined public, if they believe the death penalty as it used to be carried out was something that did not benefit this country and did much harm because it diverted attention from the causes of crime, their voices should be raised for abolition. I praise the courage of those people who continue to write-theirs is a more slender stream of letters than from those who support the death penalty-but they should continue to write and urge the total and final abolition of capital punishment in this country.
Can we go back after a generation without capital punishment? The country has changed a lot in that time, particularly the minority groups and native people. Now there are demands for nations within the nation-but how much greater this would be if we returned to capital punishment and the federal government attempted to carry out that sentence without exception? A return to capital punishment would speed the demand for nations within the nation. Within the last two weeks there has been a suicide which has been widely published and is being called a martyrdom. Imagine the tensions that would arise if we were trying to execute a member of the native population. In Vancouver, at the moment, an extradition case is being argued and tensions are rising, although in a sense it is somebody else's problem. These are things we have to consider, Mr. Speaker. The women's liberation movement has made great strides, but I wonder if they would argue for the right to hang women when it has been so long denied them.
I reply to the women who talk to me, write to me and are vehemently in favour of the death penalty, that no woman in the country should argue for capital punishment, partly for the reason I have just mentioned, and for other reasons. Women have been the great exception. For many years half the population has been automatically exempt from the death penalty, not by reason of law but by reason of our custom, tradition, the benevolence of our courts and the kindness of juries. Women have been exempt from the penalty, and the exemption has remained.
The question of the death penalty is closely related to the question of abortion, another tough question which parliament may need to consider again. I get letters which say, in so many words, "Abortion is murder." It seems to me that the public which is aroused about the death penalty and prepared to see a return of the death penalty may also become aroused about the scandal of abortion and seek to change the law in that regard. It seems to me that since some women call abortion murder, and others a matter only for the woman involved and her doctor, there is a split in the nation, a split which a referendum will not settle. I say that because you would have to argue whether men would have the right to vote in that referendum.

May 26, 1976

While we have been arguing whether to retain the death penalty or abolish it, we have not been at all prepared to abandon our thirst for violence as depicted on the media. In this country and in the country to the south of us we have been steeped, hour by hour, day by day and week by week in a compendium of violence and crime on television which has influenced for more than a generation virtually every child growing up on this continent. We have not been prepared to remove those instructions in violence from our television sets, but have freely sat in front of our sets and enjoyed the stories of violent death and murder in every conceivable shape and form. Then we wonder, as we reap some of the harvest of that depicted violence, whether we should retain the death penalty, whether we should say, "Let us return to capital punishment", and try to clean up a situation which has been spawned by a variety of causes.
It is essential for members of parliament to vote on this issue according to their conscience; and I include the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the cabinet. Since this subject is of the utmost importance to the public, I suggest that we ought to be debating a resolution, not a bill. Certainly, we ought not to be debating two bills concerned with so vital an area. The people should trust their elected representatives to vote either for or against abolition. I know that some call for a national referendum on the subject; but a national referendum is not part of the parliamentary tradition we inherited from Great Britain. It was not to the credit of former prime minister Harold Wilson that he employed a referendum in connection with Britain's entry to the Common Market. It was unnecessary, and a waste of public money. Fortunately for Mr. Wilson, the results of the referendum agreed with the vote in parliament.
We should recall, as well, Mackenzie King's referendum on conscription. That referendum raised more questions than it answered and was not followed by legislation based on the results obtained. Therefore, a referendum is unsatisfactory, and until the constitution is changed the ultimate responsibility for action rests in this House. It is our duty to act as the representatives of the people.
This is not a convention of delegates. This is a parliament. It is our duty to debate and then to legislate. If we received our instructions automatically from our constituents, debate would be unnecessary. We would await the results of the polls on any topic and become mere ciphers, carrying out the instructions of our constituents. We do not do this; that is the glory of our parliamentary system.
Let me now say a word about the churches. I have received letters arguing both sides of this question, but have been astonished, after reading some of the letters, to note that they are signed by a minister or a pastor of a church. I am afraid I am not much good at quoting scripture chapter and verse. I had a formidable grandmother who preached endless sermons to me, my brothers and sister; she could quote chapter and verse endlessly. Perhaps, because she did it so well, I have never been able to do it at all. But one thing she did say: her Christianity was based on the New Testament, not on the old law. She told us time and again that the old law was written for our admonition, but our instructions lay in the New Testament.
Capital Punishment
I still cannot understand why those who study Christ's life and devote their life to His service cannot stand back a bit, so to speak, from the narrow language of chapter and verse and let the glow of the stories of the New Testament light their way through life. Surely that is a better ideal. One remembers many stories. I cannot tell you in which part of the Gospels these stories are to be found; some of them need to be examined thoughtfully, from a little distance. I think, first, of the story concerning the rejection of political power. Christ was taken to the top of the mountain and shown the whole world. I suspect if He had heeded the teachings of some of our modern-day churches, He would have said at the top of the mountain, "Here is a chance to clean up the world." By doing that He would have accepted temptation, rather than rejecting it. But He rejected political power and chose the different route. I think also of the beautiful story in which He commuted the death sentence of the woman taken in adultery. The law called for death and He commuted the sentence at some risk to Himself, because the group which was about to stone her to death was in the heat of passion and thirsted for blood. He dared to commute the woman's sentence. I think of the beatitude of the noble sentiment enshrined in that story: Blessed are the merciful, for they shall find mercy.
I think of the story, perhaps most crucial of all but seldom referred to in this context, of that crazed individual in the cemetery. We do not know if he was guilty of murder; he was guilty of something, perhaps of disturbing the peace. He had been chained, put in the maximum security institution of the day, but still had broken out. Nobody dared to touch him. One suspects the worst about his background. The scripture is silent on that point. The stories of the New Testament teach us that Christ permitted no man or woman to be regarded as an animal, not even one who had been treated as a beast. And I get letters from constituents saying we should sort out the animals from the people. They fail to see how closely interwoven the two can be. But Christ talked to that strange person; nobody had the courage to go with him. Then, when the curious crowd gathered round, they found the sinner seated and in his right mind. There was no suggestion that he needed to serve the rest of his sentence. His rehabilitation was complete and final.
Of course, Christ himself was eventually the victim of capital punishment. Pontius Pilate took a poll. That is something that people forget. He was given the answer very quickly; it was Barabbas. He responded to that impromptu poll. Gallup comes later. We should not forget that part. We should not forget the crucifixion between two common criminals, because that was not accidental. He was numbered with the transgressors. I will not go into the theological difficulties and the "ifs" and the "ors", because what was done was done. It should serve to illuminate the debate going on at the present time.
I have a concern for all the victims, whether it is the battered wife hit too hard once after years and years of battering, whether it is the so-called unfaithful wife, or whether it is somebody beaten to death by somebody while in a drunken stupor. I have a regard for those victims. It

May 26, 1976
Capital Punishment
has been a long, long time in this country that a life has been demanded for a life in those circumstances.
If any women in this country feel strongly about it, they should read "Crimes of Passion" in the July, 1975, issue of Chatelaine, by Barbara Amiel. She writes well on that subject. She writes about the problem of domestic quarrels, the integrity of the law and concludes with this paragraph: But perhaps the integrity of the law might be better maintained if we called a spade a spade and a murder a murder and started indicating that our society will not consider the marriage license a discount certificate for reduced rates in case of violence.
One thing is certain; it must be abolition or it must be broader. This is part of what we face. Those who demand a much greater broadening of capital murder have a point because it would make much more sense if it were all or none. We must leave no crack open. In the law as it now is, two cracks were left open. The hope was that no one would dare squeeze through, but they have done so in surprising numbers. Out of that grew a dilemma. Therefore, we must not close off those two and open one more. Here I would refute the argument about the second murder because somebody will squeeze through that very swiftly. Then all the arguments that apply to the first murder will apply to the second: Was it accidental; was it premeditated? All that will arise again and we will have achieved nothing. Sooner than we think we will be back into debate once again.
Would we be able to resist the demands of television to televise executions? We can hardly resist the demand to televise the proceedings in this chamber. If television can enter here and change it as it will inevitably change the role of this institution, how long can we deny the camera access to executions themselves and with results that are not predictable? A great many people say there would be a revulsion if hangings were televised across the nation. I am sure there would be a revulsion if we returned to capital punishment. However, if they were televised, I wonder whether we have not become so depraved that we could enjoy, as a mass, those spectacles. One cannot predict the effects of television. Therefore, I urge that we abandon capital punishment once and for all, altogether, completely and utterly, so that we will not have this ritual sacrifice.
When there have been so few people executed, the executions are in a sense rituals, a sacrifice for the sins of all. Getting back to the church, that has not been necessary for over 1,900 years. Once and for all, the final sacrifice for the sins of the world was made. If we listen to the story at all, we cannot deny the redemptive power that comes through that sacrifice. We should remove capital punishment once and for all and work toward building a society where the causes of murder are removed. We should work toward educating our people to do no murder in this land.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to the encouragement of some of my constituents to vote to abolish the barbarism of capital punishment, I can only relate to this House what my conscience tells me to do and how my present state of mind was reached. Throughout my youth I attended many policy sessions and so-called "think tanks" on the issue of capital punishment. In each and every case I voted in favour of the perennial resolutions for the abolition of capital punishment. However, for better or for worse, I became a Crown attorney in the year 1970.

During my four years as a prosecutor I had the misfortune to assist in the prosecution of a West Saint John, New Brunswick, man who was convicted of having murdered a seven-year old child. During the commission of the murder, a sexual assault took place on the person of the young and innocent girl. I did not feel then, nor do I feel now, that society could afford the luxury of keeping the perpetrator of such a heinous crime alive. The possibility, however remote, exists that the murderer in this case will be released into our midst at some time in the future.
The question that preyed upon my conscience then, as it does now, is: What should be done to such an individual? After considerable thought, some of it during restless hours of the night, the answer came to me that he should be executed-not hanged, but put to death in the most humane way possible. My thoughts on the issue of capital punishment were solidified when a short time later, as prosecutor, I was obliged to attend the autopsy of a five-year old girl who was murdered in the Saint John area. Assuming the perpetrator of this foul deed, who was never apprehended, was found to be legally sane and convicted, he too, in my humble opinion, should be put to death.
I wish that I had not been exposed to these two cases. Also, I wish that compassion for this type of killer could prevail over what my conscience tells me to do. However, that not being the case, I shall cast my ballot against the abolition of the death penalty, bearing in mind that its use should be restricted to a very small number of cases. It is my submission that the state should have the right to decide when the lives of certain criminally-ill murderers should be terminated. I should like to point out, Mr. Speaker, that I am pleased to see the issue being put to a free vote.
In conclusion, may I emphasize that I understand the principles of abolitionists, even though my conscience does not allow me to embrace these principles. I trust that the same understanding will flow from abolitionists to me.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, many members who have participated in this debate have referred to its repetitive nature. To me this only suggests that uncertainty surrounds an issue which has moral overtones. It also suggests to me that the Canadian public has hardly made up its mind on the question of retention or abolition of capital punishment. There is great confusion and profusion of divergent viewpoints.
I think one of the reasons this has persisted over such a long period of time-as some hon. members have indicated, this is the third time we have debated the issue, with inconclusive results-is that the government of the day has failed to provide basic leadership on what I regard as the fundamental function and responsibility of government, and that is the maintenance of peace, order and good government. The style of the present government has had a strong determining influence on the mood of the nation. It has been a style of government that has induced a permissive attitude toward the basic subject of peace, order and good government. Indeed, up until the appearance of Bill C-83, the so-called peace and security legislation, the leadership of the government has been entirely in a permissive direction-easy bail, murders committed while murderers
May 26, 1976

are out on bail, failure on the part of the government to carry out the law that exists and as it has been determined in two successive free votes in the House of Commons. In other words, the government has failed to accept its responsibilities, and as a result we see this continuing confusion revealed in the debate which is taking place in this House.
We are now back to another free vote. But I wonder, Mr. Speaker, whether it will be a free vote when every member of the cabinet votes, as the cabinet did last time, for the abolitionist position. It seems to me that rather than being a free vote, this is following the principle of cabinet solidarity. I think it would be more to the point if ministers of the Crown, members of the treasury benches, were allowed to follow their conscience in this issue as well as the backbench members of the House of Commons.
My position over the years has been expressed in the attitude of the government of which I was a part in the early 1960s, which was to divide the punishment for homicide, for the capital offence, into two categories, that of capital murder and non-capital murder. Many members during the course of this debate-some have followed the same tack this afternoon-have stated that the possibility of condemning an innocent man to death is one of the reasons they are voting for absolute abolition. Others argue-the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leg-gatt) made this point-that very serious injustice would be done in cases of this kind. However, Mr. Speaker, with the two categories of murder-which have actually been the law, with slight amendments, up to the present time-any possibility of condemning an innocent man would be done away with absolutely, because capital punishment, the ultimate penalty, would only be administered to those who were syndicated criminals, those who use crime as part of their daily activity-the paid "hit men", the professional gunmen who are appearing with greater frequency in some of our major cities in Canada, as they have in the United States in recent years.
It is a fact-this has been demonstrated in the reports of the Law Reform Commission-that most murders are committed by murderers who are acquainted with their victims. They are domestic crimes-husband and wife, lovers, "friends"; I put that in quotation marks-people of this sort. These murders come under the category of crimes of passion. Under the legislation as it existed in the time of the Diefenbaker government, this type of homicide was tried under the non-capital murder provisions of the Criminal Code.
The question of deterrence has appeared repeatedly. I am not going to argue whether capital punishment deters the crime of homicide; I do not think it does. When you are dealing with the heinous, horrendous kinds of capital murder which would be dealt with under the capital punishment aspects of the Criminal Code, you are, of course, dealing with psychopathic personalities, people without conscience, people who have no compunction about murdering someone. There is absolutely no possibility of their being deterred even by the threat of the ultimate penalty. The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt) gave some striking examples from her own personal experience of this sort of psychopathic criminal.
Capital Punishment
Mr. Speaker, I have had occasion to deal with one such person on a personal basis in the police courts in Toronto back in 1940, and it has had a strong determining influence over the years on the attitude that I have taken toward this issue. The case in point was that of the silk-stocking murder. Bill Newell, a handsome member of the Royal Canadian Air Force, in the early days of the war cut a wide swath in criminal activity in the various places he was stationed across Canada. I came to know Bill Newell in my capacity as a social worker in Toronto and was amazed to find that there was a genuine psychopathic personality, as handsome as a Greek god but without any social conscience or awareness whatever in regard to the crime of murder. He wound up murdering his wife on Centre Island in Toronto in the famous silk-stocking murder.
As the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway pointed out, there is, unfortunately, in our society this category of psychopathic personality. What are we going to do with them, Mr. Speaker? As I shall try to point out as I move along in this debate this afternoon, when it comes to the question of vengeance putting a criminal of this kind away for 25 years, for life imprisonment, it is much more cruel, much more punitive, much more vengeful than execution through the due process of the law.
[DOT] <1740)
I am arguing the case this afternoon from the legal aspect, not from the religious aspect or from any other aspect that might be involved. I am sure we are all abolitionists at heart, wishing we lived in a society where there was no crime and in a world where there was no war. My generation had to make a decision with the onslaught of the Nazi holocaust in 1940. Some of us were pacifists who believed that war was the ultimate evil, and had even signed the Oxford resolution that under no circumstances should we take up arms for king and country, because man was just too good, with the hope that there would never be any more warfare. We had to make the decision whether we would serve, or refuse, on the basis of our sense of social responsibility.
We do not yet live in our utopias, even though we dream of the day of a utopia when the lion will lie down with the lambs and man shall beat his sword into a plowshare and will not make war against our fellowman. Some of those who seek utopia tell us the golden age is just around the corner, but some of these are the worst criminals in the political and judicial sense. I refer to what has taken place in the U.S.S.R. and in Nazi Germany where genocide and mass murder were perpetrated within our own living memory in the interest of carrying out so-called humanitarian justice.
Our system of justice involves a social contract that citizens enter into voluntarily with the understanding that society will protect them. It becomes a very sorry travesty of justice, and it has not happened in Canada but it could according to present trends, when communities of senior citizens are forced to surround themselves with electrified, barbed-wire fences, patrolled 24 hours a day by security guards, in order to keep out marauders and potential criminals. It is almost like putting the senior citizens in jail and allowing the criminals to run rampant in the community and in society.

May 26, 1976
Capital Punishment
What are the methods of handling criminals? At one time society used to ban their criminals, getting rid of them-out of sight, out of mind-by sending them to colonies such as Australia, Canada and notorious Devil's Island. More recently, we have been listening to social scientists and social engineers who believe that all crime has environmental causes, and men and women are criminals because we live in a sick society. They advocate the rehabilitation route for solving the crime problem.
The rehabilitation program has had strong support during our discussion of the subject from time to time in the House of Commons. We must face the sad fact that as we move toward rehabilitation versus the punitive approach, we are faced with the continuing phenomenon of crime repetition or recidivism. Recidivism is a fact, and this can be demonstrated by the prison population which remains at a constant 20,000 inmates, or at least has from the years 1969 to 1974, notwithstanding our system of parole, probation and temporary leaves of absence. It has been demonstrated by scientific analysis that many of these 20,000 inmates are repeaters with numerous sentences behind them.
If this is so, we must point out to our social engineers that prisons cause crimes. This would be true, of course, if the environmental theory is accurate. So this leads to the next approach to solving the criminal problem, and that is to empty the prisons. This is one of the major recommendations of the Law Reform Commission set up by the federal government under the Law Reform Commission Act of 1970 to recommend changes in Canadian law. The Law Reform Commission has been a most powerful advocate of dismantling or downgrading prisons. Some of these recommendations issued in the working papers now before us have been pretty radical. I give as an example the recommendation of a maximum three-year sentence for those violent murderers unlikely to repeat their crime. I challenge any social engineer or social scientist to tell us which of the psychopathic murderers are those who will not repeat their crime.
The law commission has also recommended no greater imprisonment for most violent criminals, and no more life sentences. I mention that because the government, in its attempt to trade off the issue of capital punishment for peace and security, has got itself into a cleft stick. It has been repudiated by the very commission it set up to examine the present state of Canada's criminal law.
If the Law Reform Commission is advocating that we empty our prisons and that there be no more life sentences, how is it that the Justice Department and the Department of the Solicitor General are recommending that we deal with first-degree murder-the imposition of a mandatory life sentence, and for second-degree murder or crimes of passion, which anyone is liable to fall into, but for the grace of God, as John Wesley said-with sentences of up to ten years?
It has been suggested that murder is on the increase, and certainly statistics point in that direction. In 1961, the last year capital punishment was imposed, there were 185 murders, and in 1974 there were 545 murders perpetrated in Canada. This being true, what are we going to do with the recommendation by the social engineers, who have the ear of the government, that we do away with penal institu-

tions completely and divert the prison population back into the community?
There is an interesting article which appears in the current Quest magazine outlining the position of Mr. Hans Mohr, a member of the crime commission. He is one of the strongest advocates of doing away with incarceration of criminals. This is the schizophrenic attitude of the government, and this is why parliament is in a schizophrenic mood with members debating the issue almost in both directions simultaneously. How can we bring about rehabilitation in penal institutions, if penal institutions are basically the cause of crime and recidivism is caused mainly by the atmosphere in our existing penal institutions?
There seems to be anarchy in our prisons today. This is mentioned in the report of the crime commissioners. An editorial in the Globe and Mail states that our prisons are becoming a no-man's land beyond the rule of law and civilized man. The Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) has said that the situation in the prisons today is such that it is necessary to break up cliques and gangs and transfer them to other institutions. Yet the government intends to deal with the ultimate crime of murder by sending psychopathic and professional murderers, syndicated murderers and paid killers, to our penal institutions-which have been roundly condemned-for a mandatory life sentence of 25 years.
Obviously, Bill C-84 is a backward move in this regard. If the atmosphere is bad now, what will it be when we have an increasingly larger population of murderers serving life sentences let loose in our penal institutions? If we are to solve the problem, it will be necessary to have special institutions because the lives of the guards will not be worth anything. This is why parliament, the last time it voted, provided an exemption for prison guards and police officers. This will create an absolutely intolerable and impossible situation. As I have already indicated, the trade-off is more cruel than the death penalty itself. It would be a living death for first-degree murderers, and even second-degree murderers would be living in an impossible situation. It seems to me that by the present legislation the government is removing one nightmare and replacing it with another that has even more dire consequences for people.
I wish to spend the last minutes of my presentation this afternoon dealing with the victims of crime. Almost exclusively we are talking about criminals.The Solicitor General has bought, almost without reservation, the argument of the social engineers and social scientists. He agonizes over the psychological strain of imprisonment referred to by the social engineers and shares the worry of the Law Reform Commission which expresses itself in similar words by referring to the anxiety which can be induced by incarceration.
Curiously, the Solicitor General is less concerned about the psychological anxiety of society at large. While the social engineers have been studying the psyches of convicts, a similar study of their victims and a most cursory look at the Gallup polls and letters to the editors which members receive on this subject from the majority of their
May 26, 1976

constituents will indicate the far more dangerous psychological trauma of society.
I have already referred to the citizens' group that had to surround itself with barbed wire and hire security guards for protection against criminal attack. The Solicitor General has an almost mystical belief in social science and social scientists, notwithstanding the fact that his own departmental people can prove to him that the results of last week had been anticipated with regard to the impact of rehabilitation. He perceives the criminal as a person suffering from a lack of love early in life, who rebels with anti-social behaviour, and he simply cannot believe that criminals are other than sick people. I would point out to him that there are psychologists who have underscored this as a psychopathic situation where the human spirit has been so warped that nothing less than being born again would take out the kinks from these unfortunate victims of our society.
Even the physical scientists today are not so sure they have all the answers in the realm of the material and the physical. At one time they had all the answers. The chemical engineers have discovered that their attempts to change the material environment by miracle sprays and chemicals have had an impact that they could not possibly anticipate. There are no more modest people today than the physical scientists who no longer play the role of God even in a material world. So, I should like to say a word on
Capital Punishment
behalf of the victims and the traumas they experience in the face of the awful crime of first-degree murder.
Finally, to bring my remarks to a conclusion and coming back to the basic issue of peace, order and good government, we are hosting the Olympic games this year. This has been brought up in the House before by one of our most distinguished members. What happens if terrorism is cut loose at the Olympic games, and what if some of the terrorists are apprehended and are incarcerated in our prisons even though the crime might be subject to capital punishment? What happens if hijackings of aircraft ensue in order to attempt the blackmail release of these imprisoned terrorists?
Surely the state has the right to protect itself against those who are out to destroy the integrity of the state. Peace, order and good government must be preserved. It cannot be preserved if we condone the use of the ultimate crime, capital murder, by those who would destroy our way of life deliberately-not those involved in crimes of passion but those who would deliberately set out to destroy our way of life. This is why I support the retention of capital punishment for those who are guilty of first-degree capital murder.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
